title: The Gang Solves Global Warming

jokes.text: Mac declaring global warming is 'all a part of God's plan' and that if God wants to roast us like turkeys, there's got to be a good reason for it
jokes.setup: The gang is discussing the very real, urgent threat of global warming and climate change
jokes.punchline: Mac deflects the existential crisis with cheerful theological fatalism — 'if God wants to roast us like turkeys, there's got to be a good reason for it'
jokes.explanation: Classic Mac move — immediately collapsing a serious real-world issue into his blind religious devotion. 'Roast us like turkeys' is a great specific image. High character integration because only Mac would say this; it establishes his arc for the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Look, if God wants to roast us like turkeys, there's got to be a good reason for it.

jokes.text: 'That's easy for you to say; you're young. You know who's gonna get hurt the worst? Old people.' — 'No, it's the younger generation that's gonna suffer from global warming the most.'
jokes.setup: Mac has just dismissed global warming as God's plan
jokes.punchline: Frank immediately makes climate change about himself (as an old person who will suffer), while someone else argues it's the younger generation — both are missing the point entirely
jokes.explanation: Functional joke about selfish people making a global crisis about personal grievances. Frank's self-centeredness is well-established, but this isn't a particularly sharp execution of that trait.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: when opinions meet facts, that's when you get truth.

jokes.text: 'Well, yes, the 25 years of climate science finally caught up with my opinions, and, Dennis, when opinions meet facts, that's when you get truth.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is saying they're all finally in agreement that climate change is real
jokes.punchline: Dennis frames this as the science catching up WITH HIM — his opinions preceded the facts, and their union produces 'truth' — classic narcissistic Dennis logic
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional Dennis Reynolds characterization. The joke is structurally perfect: he's agreeing with everyone while simultaneously centering himself as the arbiter of truth. 'When opinions meet facts, that's when you get truth' is a brilliantly constructed piece of pseudo-intellectual nonsense that sounds almost logical. It's quotable, it's character-specific, and it rewards careful listening. Among the best lines in the episode.

dialogue.line: Oh, God.

jokes.text: The gang spontaneously breaks into singing and dancing to 'The Heat Is On' in the bar in response to Dennis's motivational speech
jokes.setup: Dennis gives an earnest 'we can all work together' speech ending with 'Guys, we can beat the heat'
jokes.punchline: The gang immediately and unironically bursts into the Glenn Frey song with full energy, completely undermining the gravity of the speech
jokes.explanation: A reliable Always Sunny bit — the gang doing something absurd in unison. The song choice is on-the-nose obvious, which slightly undercuts it, but the energy of the moment and the juxtaposition with serious climate discussion earns a decent laugh.

dialogue.line: Group singing 'The Heat is On' while customers swelter

jokes.text: Frank's immediate objection to the AC plan: 'I don't know why we're wasting our AC on strangers.'
jokes.setup: Dennis explains his genius plan to help the environment AND the bar by cranking the AC
jokes.punchline: Frank's first instinct is not environmental concern or business logic, but pure misanthropy — strangers don't deserve their AC
jokes.explanation: Perfect Frank economy — one sentence that reveals his entire worldview. The misanthropic twist on what should be a 'good for business' response is very Frank. High economy score because it does so much with so little.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I don't know why we're wasting our AC on strangers.

jokes.text: Dee explains her eco-friendly shoe Instagram Story where she shames people for not having them, then says 'You know, you remember.'
jokes.setup: Dee is explaining her eco-warrior approach to environmentalism
jokes.punchline: 'You know, you remember' — delivered with complete sincerity, assuming anyone watched her Instagram Story when obviously no one did
jokes.explanation: Good Dee joke — her delusion about her own social media relevance is a recurring source of comedy. 'You know, you remember' landing in dead silence is the real punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Like I do with my shoes, you know what I mean?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: How would I know what you mean?

jokes.text: 'Who the fuck do you think is watching your... What?!' / 'Not-not one person on Earth is...'
jokes.setup: Dee assumes everyone watched her Instagram Story about eco-shoes
jokes.punchline: Mac and Charlie's overlapping disbelieving reactions — the audience assumes nobody watches Dee's stories, confirmed by their incredulous responses
jokes.explanation: The reaction beat is the punchline here. Mac's interrupting 'What?!' is well-timed and the overlapping denials compound the joke about Dee's lack of an audience. Functional cringe comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Who the fuck do you think is watching your... What?!

jokes.text: 'Plus, how is there any plastic left in the ocean after they used it to cover your gargantuan feet?'
jokes.setup: Dee is bragging about her recycled-plastic eco shoes
jokes.punchline: Mac pivots to insulting the size of her feet — the eco shoes depleted the ocean's plastic supply just to cover them
jokes.explanation: A solid two-step joke: start with an environmental concern (plastic in the ocean), pivot to a personal insult (Dee's big feet). The logic is tight enough to earn it. 'Gargantuan' is a good word choice.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: how is there any plastic left in the ocean after they used it to cover your gargantuan feet?

jokes.text: Dennis uses incentivizing Charlie with free cat food to get him to accompany Dee on the ice errand
jokes.setup: Dennis is explaining how to incentivize people to make good environmental decisions
jokes.punchline: Charlie's entire cooperation is purchased with the promise of free Purina cat food — his weirdest running characteristic deployed as a plot device
jokes.explanation: The cat food running gag is a reliable Always Sunny staple. Using it here as an environmental incentive metaphor is clever structural deployment — Dennis is literally demonstrating his theory using Charlie's cheapest desire.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: make more waste by having a big smoke-spewing truck deliver ice to us when we could just simply get off our asses and go get it ourselves?

jokes.text: Dennis asks Frank what temperature causes a certain body part's smooth muscle cells to contract and protrude 'in an unusual fashion' — Frank immediately answers '65.7 degrees Fahrenheit'
jokes.setup: Dennis is trying to incentivize Frank to cooperate by offering to lower the AC
jokes.punchline: The elaborate scientific circumlocution turns out to be about nipples, which Frank answers with terrifying specificity: exactly 65.7 degrees
jokes.explanation: Two-part joke with great construction. First layer: Dennis's hilariously over-elaborate medical description of what is simply 'cold makes nipples hard.' Second, better layer: Frank's instant, confident, specific answer of '65.7 degrees Fahrenheit' — implying he has thought about this extensively and knows the exact number. The specificity of the decimal is what elevates this from a decent joke to a great one.

dialogue.line: We'll do a Story about Purina, tag them, and get you a free case of cat food.

jokes.text: 'Nipples, Mac. Uh, nipples.' — delivered to Mac who was left out of the whole exchange
jokes.setup: Mac has been standing there confused while Dennis and Frank had the cryptic nipple conversation
jokes.punchline: Dennis's flat, almost bored explanation: 'Nipples, Mac. Uh, nipples.' followed by an unnamed woman saying 'Hi'
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — the entire punchline is two words repeated with an 'uh' between them. The flat delivery of 'nipples, Mac. Uh, nipples.' followed by a random woman saying 'Hi' (presumably someone whose nipples are now visible) is a great button on the bit. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Frank, what's the temperature at which a certain body part's small, smooth muscle cells contract, thereby decreasing the surface area of the skin, causing that certain body part to protrude in an unusual fashion?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: 65.7 degrees Fahrenheit.

jokes.text: 'Son of a bitch charged me $40 for a bag of ice, Charlie. He's taking advantage of this heat wave, jacking up the prices.' — Charlie: 'Yeah, he's smart.'
jokes.setup: Dee is outraged at being price-gouged for ice during a heat wave
jokes.punchline: Charlie's immediate, genuine admiration for the price-gouger: 'Yeah, he's smart.' — with no irony intended
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom button — straight man expects commiseration, gets sincere admiration for the villain. Charlie's moral compass pointing directly at 'that's actually smart' is very character-consistent and the economy of his response is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Son of a bitch charged me $40 for a bag of ice, Charlie. They... he's taking advantage of this heat wave, jacking up the prices.

jokes.text: Dee's feet are blistered and swollen in her eco-friendly shoes, but she says 'they're so cute and totally on-brand'
jokes.setup: Dee's eco shoes are causing her visible pain — she's limping
jokes.punchline: Despite the obvious physical suffering, her only concern is the aesthetic and brand alignment: 'they're so cute and totally on-brand'
jokes.explanation: Good Dee joke — her vanity and social media obsession overriding actual physical pain. Slightly predictable but well-executed. The 'on-brand' language is period-appropriate and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah, he's smart.

jokes.text: Charlie's Instagram Story direction: Dee says 'staged moments that looked candid and seemed honest' vs. what Charlie understood as 'candid moments that seemed honest'
jokes.setup: Charlie is filming Dee's eco-journey for Instagram and captures her limping and complaining
jokes.punchline: Dee corrects him — she wanted 'staged moments that LOOKED candid' — the precise opposite of actual honesty, delivered as if it's a reasonable distinction
jokes.explanation: Sharp media satire embedded in character comedy. 'Staged moments that looked candid and seemed honest' is an incisive skewering of influencer authenticity performance, delivered by Dee with total sincerity. The distinction between her instructions and Charlie's understanding is a great small joke.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I said staged moments that looked candid and seemed honest.

jokes.text: Dee explains rideshare — 'It's when a bunch of people get the app, and then y'all take the same vehicle to different places.' Charlie: 'Same vehicle, diff... so, like a bus.'
jokes.setup: Dee insists they can't take the disgusting bus but proposes a rideshare instead
jokes.punchline: Charlie immediately and correctly identifies that a rideshare is functionally a bus — 'same vehicle, diff... so, like a bus' — exposing Dee's classism masquerading as innovation
jokes.explanation: One of the sharper jokes in the episode. Charlie's dawning realization that a rideshare is 'like a bus' is both a great character moment (Charlie being accidentally insightful) and genuine social commentary on how the tech economy repackaged public transit for people who think they're above it. The 'same vehicle, diff—' stutter as his brain catches up is perfect timing. 'So, less room' as a follow-up makes it even better.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Do you have any idea how much pollution a bus causes?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I don't know. Uh, three? Three what? Pollutions?

jokes.text: Charlie's pollution measurement: 'I don't know. Uh, three?' / 'Three?' / 'Three what?' / 'Pollutions?'
jokes.setup: Dee argues against taking the bus because of the pollution it causes.
jokes.punchline: Charlie offers 'three' as the amount of pollution a bus causes, then, when pressed, doubles down with 'Pollutions?' — revealing he has no concept of environmental metrics whatsoever.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The escalation is perfect: Charlie ventures a confident guess of 'three,' then when challenged on what unit, invents the word 'Pollutions?' with a question mark. It's pure Charlie — unashamed ignorance, a made-up unit, and total commitment. The structure is tight and the character integration is flawless. 'Pollutions?' is highly quotable and very Charlie. Fully justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Yeah. It's when a bunch of people get the app, and then y'all take the same vehicle to different places. Same vehicle, diff...

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: so, like a bus.

jokes.text: Dee: 'Fine, but it's not a bus, it's a car. So less room.' Charlie: ''Cause if we just take the bus...' Dee: 'WE'RE NOT TAKING A BUS, CHARLIE!'
jokes.setup: Charlie has logically cornered Dee on the rideshare-is-a-bus argument
jokes.punchline: Dee's response to being out-argued by Charlie is to double down — 'it's a car, so less room' — an objectively WORSE option, delivered with authority, then screaming when Charlie presses it
jokes.explanation: Good escalation on the previous joke. Dee's logic trap — insisting on the car EVEN THOUGH it has less room — is perfect hypocrisy comedy. The screaming is earned by the buildup. Charlie's patient 'cause if we just take the bus...' re-entry is great.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Uh, well, they go to my church. And if I kick them out, then they'll tattle on me to God.

jokes.text: Mac's explanation for why he can't kick out the fish factory workers: 'They go to my church. And if I kick them out, then they'll tattle on me to God.'
jokes.setup: Dennis tells Mac to kick out the smelly fish factory workers who are driving away customers
jokes.punchline: Mac refuses not on principle but because they'll 'tattle on him to God' — framing God as a kind of divine hall monitor who receives complaints from church members
jokes.explanation: Brilliant reduction of Mac's religiosity. Rather than any theological reasoning, Mac's God-fear is essentially social — he doesn't want to be ratted out. 'Tattle on me to God' is a highly quotable, perfectly Mac-specific phrase. The bureaucratic/playground framing of divine judgment is very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Now is not the time for your racism. This affects us all. We're all in this together.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Talking about the nipples.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I don't see any.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Oh.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Right, right. Sorry. Your, um... Not... people.

jokes.text: Frank says 'I'm not very incentivized here. These are not the nips I wanted.' Dennis immediately accuses him of racism.
jokes.setup: Frank complains about not being incentivized, referring to the promised nipple display from the AC
jokes.punchline: Dennis immediately jumps to 'now is not the time for your racism' — the word 'nips' triggering a completely different interpretation. Then Frank clarifies he meant nipples, and Dennis sheepishly apologizes.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback structure. The audience knows Frank is talking about nipples (from the earlier deal), Dennis doesn't remember or mishears, and the racial slur misunderstanding creates a perfect double-take. Dennis's self-correction — 'yeah, your track record in that department is not great' — adds another layer. The fact that Dennis's first instinct was to assume racism says something about how well the show knows its characters.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's just that his misogyny is stronger than his racism. In this case.

jokes.text: 'Yeah, it's just that his misogyny is stronger than his racism. In this case.'
jokes.setup: Dennis and Mac are discussing how Frank's racism prompted Dennis to assume the worst
jokes.punchline: Mac's clinical observation that Frank's misogyny simply outranks his racism 'in this case' — said as if ranking his bigotries is a normal analytical exercise
jokes.explanation: 'In this case' is the killer qualifier — it implies they regularly rank Frank's various bigotries and this is just one data point. The analytical tone applied to something horrifying is very Always Sunny. Highly quotable as a standalone.

dialogue.speaker: Driver
dialogue.line: Well, when someone offers you gum, it's usually a hint.

jokes.text: Dee's Instagram Story: 'Hey, guys. Hey, why create an even bigger carbon footprint by taking stinky buses all over town when you can just hop in a rideshare, in an electric vehicle? I'm loving this ride, y'all.'
jokes.setup: Dee and Charlie are crammed in a hot rideshare car, visibly suffering
jokes.punchline: Dee's performed Instagram positivity — 'I'm loving this ride, y'all' — while clearly suffering in the stifling car is ironic self-parody of influencer content
jokes.explanation: Functional irony — the gap between performed enthusiasm and visible misery is a reliable comedy engine. 'I'm loving this ride, y'all' is a decent line but the joke is somewhat telegraphed at this point.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I'm gonna give you one star, jerk! Maybe consider getting some gum for those pits!

jokes.text: Charlie repeatedly saying 'And cut.' after filming Dee, then trying 'and stop.' when corrected
jokes.setup: Dee has told Charlie not to say 'and cut' when he stops filming
jokes.punchline: Charlie's workaround is to say 'and stop' — which is equally wrong and equally annoying to Dee
jokes.explanation: Good running gag with a payoff at the episode's end. Charlie's literal-minded solution (replace one word) missing the entire point is very character-appropriate. Sets up a recurring joke that escalates through the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Well, you don't want me to say 'cut,' so I'll say 'stop.' It's better.

jokes.text: 'Christ. Might as well be in a bus. I am eating this guy's breath. Just straight up eating it.'
jokes.setup: Dee insisted the rideshare was better than a bus
jokes.punchline: The rideshare is clearly worse than a bus — cramped, hot, and Dee is literally 'eating' the driver's breath — a vivid callback to her earlier complaint about buses
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback — Dee said she hated buses because of strangers 'breathing directly into your mouth,' and now she's literally doing that in the supposedly superior rideshare. 'I am eating this guy's breath. Just straight up eating it.' is a vivid, funny image.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: So we're taking two cars when we could've taken one car or called the truck and this whole thing could've been done, like, hours ago.

jokes.text: Dee asks for AC, driver says the electric car's AC kills the battery. Dee: 'Okay, then just turn it on for a minute and then turn it right back off.'
jokes.setup: They're dying of heat in the electric rideshare car
jokes.punchline: Dee's solution — turn AC on briefly then immediately off — is so logically useless it circles back to being funny
jokes.explanation: Minor joke — Dee's idiotic solution is funny but not particularly sharp. Functions as connective tissue for the rideshare sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Global warming is the fucking best.

jokes.text: Driver offers gum as a 'hint' about their breath. Dee: 'What's some gum gonna do?' Driver: 'When someone offers you gum, it's usually a hint.'
jokes.setup: Dee and Charlie are upset about the lack of AC and the driver offers gum
jokes.punchline: The driver clarifies that the gum offer is a social hint about their breath — meaning both Dee AND Charlie have bad breath
jokes.explanation: Clean little joke with a good two-step structure. The driver's clarification is matter-of-fact enough to land. The implication that BOTH passengers have bad breath adds to it.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: The Lord provideth again!

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: No, Mac! No. The Lord not provideth. Frank provideth.

jokes.text: 'That's him! That's not me.' — 'Uh, well, it's both of you. It's both of you.'
jokes.setup: Driver has implied both have bad breath
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately blames Charlie, driver confirms it's both of them — Charlie's acceptance of the blame and driver's calm confirmation
jokes.explanation: Button on the gum joke. Dee's immediate blame-deflection and the driver's calm 'it's both of you' is a solid three-beat. Functions well as a quick escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: well, the Lord provideth the snowstorm in May that allowed us to get the cups now. See? It's all a part of his divine plan, Dennis.

jokes.text: Dee gives the driver one star and tells him to 'get some gum for those pits'
jokes.setup: Driver just told Dee she has bad breath
jokes.punchline: Dee retaliates with a one-star review and tells him to use gum for his armpits — turning the gum hint back on him in an entirely wrong-headed way
jokes.explanation: Good callback — Dee weaponizes the gum hint back against the driver in the most petty way possible. 'Get some gum for those pits' is a funny line, and giving one star is very Dee. The logic is broken (gum isn't for armpits) which is the point.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: But it doesn't matter what we do if it's all predetermined. You see how your argument doesn't make any sense?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Uh, that's correct. But it doesn't have to make sense, because that's where the faith comes in.

jokes.text: Mac reports that the slow jams 'backfired' because of the friction from grinding — 'It's like all the friction from the grinding, like, created a closed system. I didn't account for all the increased sexiness.'
jokes.setup: Dennis's plan to lower body heat by playing slow jams made the bar hotter
jokes.punchline: Mac's quasi-scientific explanation: the grinding created a 'closed system' and he 'didn't account for all the increased sexiness' — said with complete earnestness
jokes.explanation: 'I didn't account for all the increased sexiness' is a legitimately great line. It's delivered with Mac's characteristic confident stupidity — he's doing a physics analysis where the variable is 'sexiness.' The pseudo-scientific framing ('closed system') elevates it above a simple dumb joke. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Well, I got a nice little trash bag... that's keeping me a little bit cooler... and then this totally creates shade. You want me to make you a hat?

jokes.text: Frank: 'Global warming is the fucking best.' — said while lounging contentedly surrounded by the chaos
jokes.setup: The bar has descended into sweaty chaos, the gang's plans have all failed
jokes.punchline: Frank, who earlier complained about wasting AC on strangers, is now having the time of his life. The existential crisis everyone else is experiencing is Frank's ideal afternoon.
jokes.explanation: Five words, perfectly Frank. After all the gang's stressed attempts to manage the situation, Frank has simply adapted and is thriving in the chaos. It's character comedy at its most economical — his entire philosophy (people are animals, there's no 'together') has been vindicated and he's comfortable. The contrast with everyone else's stress makes it land harder. 'The fucking best' as his verdict on a global catastrophe is a great line.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I can charge you for the hat if it makes you feel better.

jokes.text: Mac: 'The Lord provideth the snowstorm in May that allowed us to get the cups now. See? It's all a part of his divine plan, Dennis.'
jokes.setup: Frank points out he bought the cups for a cancelled Memorial Day party
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately retrofits a May blizzard into God's divine environmental plan — specifically so they'd have plastic cups during a heat wave six months later
jokes.explanation: Good Mac theology joke in the same vein as his earlier divine plan gags. The specificity of a May blizzard being preordained to deliver plastic cups to a Philly dive bar is a good image. Mac's total sincerity in presenting this logic is essential.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: That driver gave me one star, citing 'verbal abuse' and saying I urinated all over the backseat of his car. That was melted ice. Actually, I did pee back there a little bit.

jokes.text: Mac: 'That's correct. But it doesn't have to make sense, because that's where the faith comes in. I have faith that what I'm saying makes sense.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has just conclusively demonstrated that Mac's argument doesn't make sense
jokes.punchline: Mac concedes the argument makes no sense but deploys faith as a logical override: 'I have faith that what I'm saying makes sense' — using faith to believe in his own coherence
jokes.explanation: 'I have faith that what I'm saying makes sense' is a brilliant piece of Mac theology. It's the perfect encapsulation of using religious faith to avoid logical accountability — applied not to God or the Bible but to his own argument. The specificity of 'that what I'm saying makes sense' is what makes it exceptional. Highly quotable, very rewatchable. One of the episode's best lines.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I did, too. It was a very long ride.

jokes.text: Dennis's plan to lower body heat: 'The music — it's very up-tempo. What if we throw a couple slow jams in here? Drop the body heat down a notch.'
jokes.setup: The bar is overheating with too many people dancing
jokes.punchline: Dennis's supposedly smart solution — slow jams will lower body heat — which will immediately and obviously backfire (as confirmed in joke #28)
jokes.explanation: Setup joke whose punchline arrives later (joke #28 — the grinding created more heat). Appreciated more in retrospect. On its own, it's a mild joke about Dennis's confidence in a bad plan.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I didn't account for all the increased sexiness.

jokes.text: Mac: 'And don't you see how God came through you to come up with that idea?' — said to Dennis about the slow jams plan
jokes.setup: Dennis has just pitched what turns out to be a terrible plan (slow jams)
jokes.punchline: Mac attributes Dennis's bad idea to divine inspiration — God specifically worked through Dennis to produce a plan that will make everything worse
jokes.explanation: Good Mac joke — his religious attribution of agency extends even to Dennis's dumb plans. The irony that God's instrument is Dennis and God's plan is 'slow jams' is quietly very funny. Gets funnier in retrospect once the plan backfires.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You don't need to announce my announcement.

jokes.text: Dee: 'No, thanks. I don't want to wear trash on my head.' Charlie: 'You're wearing it on your feet.'
jokes.setup: Charlie offers to make Dee a trash-bag hat to keep her cool
jokes.punchline: Dee refuses to wear trash on her head; Charlie points out her $90 eco shoes are functionally trash too
jokes.explanation: Very economical comeback. Five words that perfectly skewer Dee's pretension — her $90 shoes made from recycled plastic are functionally trash, and Charlie's too dumb/too honest to miss the irony. Great economy score.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: I want ten shots.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You want ten shots, but, you know, ten shots is too much for you and five to six is plenty.

dialogue.speaker: Another Customer
dialogue.line: Don't tell her what she needs.

jokes.text: Dee's rideshare account has been suspended for 'verbal abuse' and because the driver claims she urinated in the backseat. 'That was melted ice.' — 'Actually, I did pee back there a little bit.' — 'I did, too.'
jokes.setup: Dee's rideshare account is suspended; she's indignant and attributes the backseat wetness to melted ice
jokes.punchline: Charlie casually admits he also urinated in the car — then Dee admits she did too — both have peed in the rideshare despite Dee's initial denial
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny escalation — Dee's moral indignation immediately collapses when Charlie's admission forces her to admit she ALSO peed in the car. 'I did, too. It was a very long ride' is a perfect Charlie line — matter-of-fact, slightly apologetic, completely unashamed. The triple-beat structure (denial, Charlie's confession, Dee's confession) is well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I got the booze!

jokes.text: Dee and Charlie are forced onto the bus. 'Goddamn it.' Cut to them arriving back — 'Oh, my God. That bus was hot as shit.'
jokes.setup: Dee has spent the entire episode refusing to take the bus on environmental and class grounds
jokes.punchline: After all her alternatives fail, she is finally forced onto the bus — multiple buses, in fact — and they are exactly as bad as she said, but for the opposite reason (heat, not germs)
jokes.explanation: Satisfying structural callback — Dee's bus avoidance arc completes with her forced onto three buses. 'The third bus was the hottest, you know what I mean?' is a funny specific detail suggesting they took multiple buses and each was worse.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: somebody ripped a hole in the bag and stole it.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Yeah. How did you not notice that?

jokes.text: Mac: 'Where is your God now?' / Frank: 'He will reveal himself at some point.' / Dennis: 'Is he gonna do it before all these people revolt and destroy the place?'
jokes.setup: The bar is chaotic, overheated, and running out of booze
jokes.punchline: Mac's rhetorical 'Where is your God now?' is immediately answered by Mac himself with sincere 'He will reveal himself at some point' — Mac can't even maintain secular despair for one line
jokes.explanation: Good running theology bit. Mac catching himself saying 'your God' and immediately defending God is a nice character moment. Dennis's practical follow-up ('before all these people revolt') keeps it grounded. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: these are our friends from the fish factory. What's up, guys? They're actually pretty good dudes once you get to know them.

jokes.text: Dennis trying to manage the increasingly unruly crowd: 'We need to chill out on the dancing a little bit... I don't want to be that guy... Let's not stop. Let's just chill out.' Gets progressively more desperate.
jokes.setup: Dennis is trying to maintain order in an overheating bar using nothing but increasingly hollow enthusiasm
jokes.punchline: Dennis's attempts to both keep the party going AND slow it down collapse into contradiction — 'Let's not stop. Let's just chill out.' — as the crowd ignores him completely
jokes.explanation: Good sustained cringe sequence. Dennis's control-freak personality meets a situation he can't manage and his language becomes increasingly incoherent — 'let's not stop, let's just chill out' is the logical impossibility at its peak. His obvious loss of authority is well-played.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: People were animals, just like I said.

jokes.text: 'I want ten shots.' Dennis: 'Ten shots is too much for you and five to six is plenty.' Unnamed woman: 'Don't tell her what she needs.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is trying to ration drinks at the overcrowded bar
jokes.punchline: A bar patron tells Dennis not to 'tell her what she needs' — Dennis's paternalistic crowd management gets challenged on feminist grounds, in a sweaty dive bar, in the middle of a climate crisis
jokes.explanation: Good ironic joke — Dennis's controlling behavior gets called out for the wrong reasons (paternalism about shot quantity rather than his actual Dennis-ness). The chaos escalating through the bar crowd works well.

jokes.text: Mac arrives with 'I got the booze!' — dissolving all of Dennis's carefully managed crowd control instantly
jokes.setup: Dennis has spent three minutes desperately trying to get people to drink less and slow down
jokes.punchline: Mac arrives with more booze, instantly undoing everything. The crowd erupts. Dennis's entire speech was for nothing.
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom button — the speech is undone by Mac's clueless arrival. 'I got the booze!' as a triumphant entrance after Dennis's desperate rationing speech is a solid visual/verbal gag. The economy of Mac's oblivious sabotage is very good.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Hope a bird chokes to death on you.

jokes.text: 'Oh, my God. That bus was hot as shit. The third bus was the hottest, you know what I mean? It's those local buses. We should've just gotten off at the express and walked.'
jokes.setup: Dee and Charlie finally return after taking multiple buses
jokes.punchline: The specificity that there were at least THREE buses, the third being the hottest, and that they had a preferred transit strategy — reveals the journey was a complete disaster they're now analyzing like experts
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'the third bus was the hottest' is what saves this — implying a progressive worsening across multiple bus rides. Their casual post-mortem about transit strategy after all their eco-pretension is a good ironic button.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I can't stand being near you low-life degenerates!

jokes.text: The ice bag was stolen — someone ripped a hole in it while Charlie carried it on his back and his back went numb so he didn't notice.
jokes.setup: Dee and Charlie finally have the ice after all their travails
jokes.punchline: The ice was slowly stolen through a hole in the bag that Charlie didn't notice because his back went numb from the ice — so the solution caused the problem
jokes.explanation: Good Sisyphean comedy — after all the hardship getting the ice, it's been gradually stolen during transit. The logic of 'my back went numb from the ice so I didn't feel the hole' is a funny self-undermining explanation. Classic Always Sunny futility.

jokes.text: Charlie: 'I got to say, though, Charlie, the feet are feeling real good. Whatever you made...' — Charlie's trash bag shoes fixed Dee's blisters
jokes.setup: Dee spent the episode in agony in her $90 eco-friendly shoes; Charlie made her trash-bag replacement shoes
jokes.punchline: The trash-bag Charlie shoes were better than the $90 eco shoes. 'I'm pretty proud of that shoe. Yeah. That's the medical sponge, which is—' 'I don't want to hear any of the details, though.'
jokes.explanation: Satisfying callback payoff — Charlie's garbage shoe beats the expensive eco shoe. 'That's the medical sponge, which is—' / 'I don't want to hear any of the details' is a good button, implying Charlie used something medical and gross.

jokes.text: Dee's feet have recovered because Charlie fashioned her shoes out of a medical sponge — she insists they feel 'real good' but won't hear the details
jokes.setup: Dee's eco-shoes destroyed her feet; Charlie improvised a solution
jokes.punchline: Charlie's medical sponge shoe is apparently effective, but Dee immediately cuts him off when he starts to describe it ('I don't want to hear any of the details, though') — implying the solution is probably disturbing
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the shoe arc. Charlie improvising footwear from a 'medical sponge' is a great image, and Dee's 'I don't want to hear any of the details' is a smart choice — the imagination is funnier than any explanation could be. Good economy.

jokes.text: Frank reports the people who were at the party were 'animals, just like I said' — but the fish factory guys are 'actually pretty good dudes once you get to know them'
jokes.setup: Frank wanted to kick out the smelly fish factory workers; Mac refused
jokes.punchline: The fish factory workers — the ones covered in fish parts who smelled terrible — turned out to be good dudes; the respectable crowd was the animals. Frank's misanthropy was correct but aimed wrong.
jokes.explanation: Thematic payoff — Frank's cynicism about people was correct but misdirected. The twist that the gross-smelling fish workers were better people than the mainstream crowd is a solid Always Sunny inversion of social expectations.

jokes.text: Dee's Instagram Story compilation: includes her screaming at the ice store owner, telling him she'll 'gouge your eyes out,' losing the ice bag argument, and ranting 'I hate the bus!'
jokes.setup: Dee is presenting her eco-influencer Instagram Story to the gang as a success
jokes.punchline: The story is an unedited disaster — screaming threats, losing arguments, cursing at bus passengers — presented as eco-advocacy content
jokes.explanation: Great payoff for Dee's whole story arc — Charlie filmed everything including all her worst moments, and they're presented as her eco-content. 'Hope a bird chokes to death on you' directed at a plastic bag, 'Not tipping you either' — the specific details are very funny. The compilation format lets all the episode's callbacks hit simultaneously.

jokes.text: Final Charlie 'And cut.' after the whole episode of Dee screaming at him about it
jokes.setup: Dee has spent the entire episode telling Charlie not to say 'and cut'
jokes.punchline: The very last thing Charlie does is say 'And cut.' — the running gag completes with Dee's exasperated 'Okay, stop saying and cut.' and Charlie's 'Goddamn it.'
jokes.explanation: Perfect running gag closer. After an entire episode of Dee screaming at Charlie about this, he still does it — and his 'Goddamn it' at the end suggests he's frustrated with HIMSELF, not Dee, which is a lovely character detail. Good economy in the resolution.

jokes.text: Final line: 'Goddamn it, Charlie.'
jokes.setup: Charlie has just said 'and stop' after being told not to say 'and cut'
jokes.punchline: Dee's resigned 'Goddamn it, Charlie' is the episode's button — total defeat, absolute futility, perfectly economical
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom button. 'Goddamn it, Charlie' as a final line works because it summarizes the entire episode's Dee/Charlie dynamic — Dee trying to execute a plan, Charlie undermining it through cheerful incompetence, Dee defeated. Three words, perfectly economical, earns its place as the closing line.

tmdb_overview: As a record-breaking heat wave overtakes Philly, the Gang plans to profit from global warming by pumping up the A/C so people will congregate at Paddy's and save energy at home.
